label: Lime, wet cement and lye (alkali burns)
summary: Quicklime, hydrated (slaked) lime, wet cement and concrete, and lye (sodium hydroxide) are strong alkalis. On damp skin and in the eyes they burn, often with little pain at first; cement burns can show hours later and keep worsening, and an eye can be blinded. Quicklime also heats up violently when it gets wet, enough to set wood or straw alight.
signs: Bags or drums of quicklime, pebble lime, hot lime or calcium oxide. Some quicklime is sold as plain 'lime' or even 'agricultural lime': check the ingredients for calcium oxide
Hydrated or slaked lime (calcium hydroxide), used in construction and water treatment
Portland cement and bagged concrete mix: mixed with water they reach pH 12–13
Crystal drain openers: one brand is 96–100% sodium hydroxide (lye)
Quicklime bags or drums that got wet: they can heat up and burst
On skin: redness, dryness, cracking, or skin turning white, yellow or black; with cement you may feel nothing until hours after contact
do: Wear waterproof, alkali-resistant gloves (nitrile, butyl or PVC), with sleeves pulled down over them

For wet concrete, wear tall rubber boots and keep it from running in over the tops: NIOSH says trousers tucked in and the boot tops taped, HSE says trousers pulled down over the boot tops. Kneel on a dry board or waterproof kneepads
Wash cement off skin at once with clean water and pH-neutral soap, not the bucket water, and change out of clothes soaked with wet cement
Keep quicklime dry in closed containers, away from water, acids and anything that burns
Dissolve lye by adding it slowly to cold water, never water onto lye, in a container that isn't aluminium
Have clean water for rinsing eyes within reach before you open a bag
dont: Don't wear contact lenses when working with lime or cement
Don't let lime, cement or concrete sit or harden against skin, or get inside gloves and boots
Don't hose down a large quicklime spill, and don't dry-sweep it: scoop it dry into a container and vacuum the fine dust with a HEPA vacuum
Don't let quicklime get wet near wood, straw or other things that burn: the heat has set them alight
Don't use lye in or near aluminium: it gives off flammable hydrogen
ppe: Chemical or indirect-vent goggles for lime and cement dust, splashes and lye; add a face shield when mixing lye
Gloves: nitrile, butyl or PVC for cement; thick butyl, nitrile, neoprene or PVC for lye, not thin ones of 0.3 mm or less
Tall rubber boots and clothing that covers arms and legs
An N95 or better when tipping lime or cement where dust hangs in the air
firstAid: Eyes: rinse at once with gently running clean water, holding the lids open and washing out every grain, away from the other eye; don't stop to remove contact lenses. Keep going at least 15 minutes for lime, 30 for cement, 60 for lye
Skin: brush off dry lime or powder first, take off soaked clothing, gloves and boots, then flush with lots of cool running water for at least 15 minutes, 60 without stopping for lye
Treat long contact with wet cement as a burn even if it doesn't hurt yet: cement burns can appear hours later and worsen after contact ends
Chemical burns to the eyes, face or a large area need medical care. If swallowed, rinse the mouth and don't make them vomit
